newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel urges German SPD to rejoin tax talks.
newsitem.headline: Waigel urges German SPD to rejoin tax talks.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Friday urged the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) to abandon their delaying tactics and rejoin cross-party talks over major tax reforms.

Introducing a 1998 tax bill to parliament which would pass the first stage of plans to cut 30 billion marks in tax, Waigel said: "The delaying tactics of the SPD are harming the common good, the unemployed and those in Germany who still have work."

The 1998 tax bill foresees cutting corporate and commercial income tax and unifying them at a common 40 percent rate in a revenue-neutral measure which would be offset by tightening up on corporate write-off possibilities.

The bill would also cut two points off the solidarity income tax surcharge to 5.5 percent, cutting 7.5 billion marks off the tax burden. The lion's share of income and corporate tax cuts would come in separate legislation for 1999.

Waigel said that with SPD cooperation it would be possible to pass the bill by July, and a 1999 tax bill by the end of the year, giving "a decisive push for a positive change of climate for doing business in Germany".

The SPD pulled out of tax talks with the coalition in a recent clash over coal subsidy cuts, and has not yet agreed to return to the negotiating table. It can block most tax measures through its majority in the upper house of parliament.
